newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka broking firms upgrade '97 EPS forecasts.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka broking firms upgrade '97 EPS forecasts.

text.p: Earnings per share (EPS) growth of Sri Lankan corporates trading on the Colombo Stock Exchange have seen sharp upward revisions for the year to December 1997, analysts said on Friday.

"EPS figures for the 12 months to December 1997 have been revised sharply upward after better than expected results in the year to March 1997," said Sanjay Kulatunga, an analyst at brokerage Jardine Fleming HNB.
Jardine Fleming has revised EPS for the year to December 1997 to 25 percent, from 18.2 percent.
The good corporate results for the year to March and the first quarter of 1997 took many by surprise, analysts said.

"Some underestimated the impact of consolidating accounts with plantations, which did exceptionally well in 1996, the upturn in tourism in the last quarter of 1996 and the first quarter of 1997," said Subram Ramaswamy, deputy general manager of Bartleet Mallory Stockbrokers.
Diversified blue chip holding companies such as John Keells Holdings, Hayleys and Aitken Spence where profits rose substantially, benefited for these reasons, he added.
Bartleet Mallory Stockbrokers has upgraded EPS forecasts for 1997 to 20 percent from 15.

John Keells Stock Brokers has upgraded EPS forecasts to 20 percent from 16, said Nandakumar Nair, the firm's research director. "We'll go with 20 percent since we do not want to be too optimistic because the market is starting from a low base."
The Colombo Stock Exchange all share index hit a three-year low when it fell below 600 points in mid-1996, after corporate results plunged when a crippling drought hit power supply and industry.
Tourism also slumped after Tamil separatists, fighting for a separate homeland in the north and east, bombed the Central Bank and a crowded commuter train.
"The year 1997 should be good because corporates seem to have got their act together and the overall economic environment seems to have improved," Ramaswamy said.
Sri Lanka's gross domestic product (GDP) growth rate which fell to 3.8 percent in 1996, is seen rising to at least 5.5 percent in 1997.
The Central Bank is confident GDP growth will hit six percent in 1997, led by improvements in agriculture and industry due to better weather conditions and uninterrupted power.

"We always said Sri Lanka would see comfortable growth in 1997 and forecast EPS growth of 15 percent for the year, which we are staying with," said Mahendra Jayasekera, general manager of brokerage CT Smith.
